The interview bar

Syntax recall vs architectural judgement

The mid-level candidate

Has memorised debounce as a snippet. Knows closures "capture variables". Can recite that class is syntactic sugar — but cannot say what it is sugar for, or what it costs at ten thousand instances.

The senior engineer

Writes the utility from the mechanism, not from memory. Knows which of scope, this, prototypes and the microtask queue is responsible for the bug on screen, and can defend the trade-off out loud while typing.

Every question in this module has the same shape: not "what does this do", but "what is the engine doing, and what did that cost".

Lesson 1 · what a call actually costs

Every function call pushes a context

const app = 'rasmi'

function outer() {
  const user = 'ahmed'
  function inner() {
    const page = 2
    return [app, user, page]   // ← all three resolve
  }
  return inner()
}
Two things are created per call: an environment record holding that call's own bindings, and a pointer to the environment where the function was defined. The pointer is the scope chain — and it is set at definition time, not call time.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 1
05 / 52
Lesson 1 · proof, in six lines

Lexical, not dynamic

const label = 'module'

function read() { return label }

function caller() {
  const label = 'caller'
  return read()
}

caller()   // → 'module'
read was written next to the module-level label, so that is the one it sees — no matter who calls it, or from where.

Three consequences worth naming

  • A missing binding walks up, never sidewaysand ends in a ReferenceError, not undefined
  • let and const exist in the record from the first linebut reading before the declaration throws — that is the temporal dead zone, not "not hoisted"
  • var is initialised to undefined insteadwhich is why the two behave differently in a loop

Not a trick question. The mechanism by which a callback still knows what it was holding when it was created.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 2
07 / 52
The definition that survives an interview

A function plus the environment it was born in

function counter() {
  let n = 0                 // lives in counter's record
  return () => ++n           // holds a reference to it
}

const a = counter(), b = counter()
a(); a()   // 1, 2
b()        // 1  — a separate record
counter returned and its stack frame popped — but its environment record did not die, because the returned function still points at it. That is the whole trick.

The classic, and why it changed

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i))
// 3, 3, 3 — one binding, shared

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i))
// 0, 1, 2 — a fresh binding per iteration

Where you already rely on it

Three shapes, one mechanism

Private state

A value only the returned functions can reach. No #private, no convention, no way to poke at it from outside.

const store = makeStore()
store.get()  // ✓
store.state  // undefined

Remembered arguments

Every partial application, every curried handler, every onClick={() => remove(id)} in a list is a closure over id.

const on = (id) =>
  () => remove(id)

A slot between calls

The timer handle in debounce, the last-run stamp in throttle, the cache in memoize. Lesson 9 is three closures and nothing else.

let t
return (...args) => {
  clearTimeout(t); ...
}
If you can explain the counter on the last slide, you can already write debounce. Lesson 9 adds the timer, not the idea.

Lesson 2 · closures as a creation strategy

Object creation without constructor coupling

A function that manufactures objects without exposing instantiation logic.
const createUser = ({ name, role, permissions = [] }) => {
  // private state hidden in closure
  const createdAt = new Date();

  return {
    name,
    role,
    can(action) {
      return permissions.includes(action) || role === 'admin';
    },
    getCreatedDate() { return createdAt; }
  };
};

const admin = createUser({ name: 'Sara', role: 'admin' });
admin.can('delete_user'); // true

When Factory Functions Excel

1 · No new Keyword: Callers can't accidentally invoke without new and pollute window.

2 · Dynamic Typing: Can return completely different object shapes based on input parameters.

3 · Pure Composition: Objects can be created by spreading mixins rather than deep class inheritance hierarchies.

10 / 52
Lesson 2 · closures vs prototypes

Factory functions vs ES6 Classes

Factory Functions

  • No this headachesMethods are arrow functions or bound closures; never lose context when passed as callbacks
  • Real encapsulationVariables in scope are truly private without needing `#` syntax
  • Easy compositionCompose behavior with Object.assign or spread

ES6 Classes

  • Memory efficientMethods live on prototype, shared across millions of instances
  • Native engine fast-pathV8 optimizes shape transitions and prototype lookups
  • instanceof checksClear type hierarchy in runtime introspection
If you need 10 instances with bulletproof callbacks: Factory. If you need 100,000 instances with high throughput: Class.

11 / 52
The other edge of the same knife

What the closure keeps alive

The cost

An environment record is reachable as long as any function that closes over it is reachable. One surviving callback can hold a 4MB response, a detached DOM node, or the whole component tree it was created in.

function attach(node) {
  const big = hugePayload()
  node.onclick = () => log('hi')
  // `big` is in the same record —
  // engines may keep it alive
}

The discipline

Keep the closed-over surface small: capture the one value you need, not the object it came from. Null out handles you own. Return an unsubscribe from anything that subscribes.

// capture the id, not the record
const { id } = job
return () => open(id)
"A memory leak is a closure that remembered something nobody asked it to." Lesson 8 measures exactly this.

Lesson 2 · what the closure costs

The hidden memory cost of closures

Creating methods inside factory functions duplicates function closures in V8 heap memory.

Factory: Methods Recreated Per Instance

If createWidget() creates 10,000 widgets and defines render() and update() inside, V8 creates 20,000 distinct function instances in memory, each with its own lexical scope closure.

Prototype: Methods Shared on Class Prototype

If class Widget defines render() and update(), V8 creates 2 function instances total on Widget.prototype. All 10,000 instances only hold a pointer to the prototype.

In frontend applications, this rarely matters for 20 UI controls. But for data tables, virtualized lists, or canvas nodes with 50,000 items, closures can exhaust browser VRAM and heap.

Read the call, not the definition

Four rules, checked in this order

function who() { return this }

who()                      // 1 · default
obj.who()                  // 2 · implicit
who.call(other)            // 3 · explicit
new Who()                  // 4 · construction
Arrow functions are not on this list. They have no this of their own — they read it from the enclosing scope, like any other variable. That is why they cannot be used as methods, and why they are perfect as callbacks.
Call shapethis is
new Fn()The new object — wins over everything
fn.call(x) / .apply / .bindx — explicit beats implicit
obj.fn()obj — whatever is left of the dot
fn()undefined in modules and strict mode; the global object in sloppy scripts
() => thisWhatever this was where the arrow was written
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 3
15 / 52
The bug you have shipped at least once

A method passed by reference loses its dot

class Search {
  query = ''
  handle(e) { this.query = e.target.value }
}

const s = new Search()
input.addEventListener('input', s.handle)
// TypeError: Cannot set property of undefined
// the listener calls handle() — no dot, no this

Three fixes, in order of preference

  • Class field with an arrowhandle = (e) => { this.query = … } — bound at construction, one per instance
  • Wrap at the call siteel.addEventListener('input', e => s.handle(e)) — nothing to remember later
  • .bind(this) in the constructorworks, but you must remember the same reference to remove the listener
Never .bind() inline in a render — a new function identity every render breaks removal, memoisation and every equality check downstream.

Lesson 3 · the receiver, at the object-model level

Why Proxy without Reflect is broken

The trap most developers fall into: using target[prop] inside a Proxy.
const parent = {
  _val: 10,
  get val() { return this._val; }
};

const proxy = new Proxy(parent, {
  get(target, prop, receiver) {
    // BUG: target[prop] executes getter with 'this === parent'
    // FIX: Reflect.get passes 'receiver' so 'this === child'
    return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver);
  }
});

const child = Object.create(proxy);
child._val = 42;
console.log(child.val); // 42 with Reflect! (10 without it!)

The Receiver Invariant

If an object has a getter method, the getter refers to this. When accessing the getter on a derived object, this MUST bind to the derived object (the receiver), not the proxy target!

Always pair Proxy with Reflect. Every Proxy trap has an identically named Reflect method that handles internal binding correctly.

Lesson 4 of 10

How JavaScript actually inherits

JavaScript is not a class-based language; it is a prototype delegation engine.
When reading user1.login(), V8 checks user1. Property missing? It walks up [[Prototype]] to User.prototype and finds it. Only if the chain hits null does it return undefined.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 4
18 / 52
Lesson 4 · delegation, without classes

Inheritance without classes or constructors

// Pure prototypal delegation
const protoUser = {
  login() { return `${this.name} logged in`; },
  hasAccess() { return this.role === 'admin'; }
};

// Create new object delegating to protoUser
const userA = Object.create(protoUser);
userA.name = 'Layla';
userA.role = 'editor';

console.log(userA.login()); // "Layla logged in"
console.log(userA.hasOwnProperty('login')); // false!
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(userA) === protoUser); // true

Differential Inheritance

userA only stores what makes it unique (name, role). All behavioral methods reside on protoUser.

This is the essence of the Prototype Pattern from the Gang of Four book: creating new objects by cloning or delegating to a prototype archetype rather than invoking heavy constructor classes.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 4
19 / 52
Lesson 4 · what class is hiding

What 'class' is actually hiding

ES6 Class Syntax
class User {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  login() {
    return this.name;
  }
}
What V8 Actually Executes
function User(name) {
  this.name = name;
}
User.prototype.login = function() {
  return this.name;
};
// User is still a function!
console.log(typeof User); // 'function'
Interview question: "Does JavaScript have true classes?"
Answer: No. Classes in JS are syntactic sugar over constructor functions and prototypal delegation chains. They introduce strict mode and block invocation without new, but the runtime inheritance model is 100% prototypal.

Lesson 4 · measured, not argued

Memory benchmark: 10,000 instances measured

Approach10,000 Objects HeapFunction Instances
Factory with Closures~18.2 MB30,000 closures
Class / Prototype~1.8 MB3 prototype methods
Object.create(proto)~1.4 MB3 prototype methods

The 90% Heap Reduction

By placing functions on the prototype instead of in instance closures, you reduce the heap allocation by an order of magnitude.

When an interviewer asks: "Why would I ever use prototype methods when closures are simpler to write?" — this table is your senior answer.

Lesson 4 · intercepting the object model

Intercept and control property access

A Proxy wraps a target object and intercepts operations using handler traps.
const user = { name: 'Omar', age: 28 };

const userProxy = new Proxy(user, {
  get(target, prop, receiver) {
    console.log(`Accessed ${String(prop)}`);
    return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver);
  },
  set(target, prop, value, receiver) {
    if (prop === 'age' && typeof value !== 'number') {
      throw new TypeError('Age must be a number');
    }
    return Reflect.set(target, prop, value, receiver);
  }
});

userProxy.age = 'thirty'; // throws TypeError!

The Core Traps

TrapTriggered By
getReading property (obj.prop)
setWriting property (obj.prop = v)
has'prop' in obj
deletePropertydelete obj.prop
applyCalling function (fn(...args))

Lesson 4 · where interception ships

How Vue 3 and MobX build reactivity

A reactive system in 12 lines of code:
let activeEffect = null;
const targetMap = new WeakMap();

function reactive(obj) {
  return new Proxy(obj, {
    get(target, key, receiver) {
      track(target, key); // collect activeEffect
      return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver);
    },
    set(target, key, val, receiver) {
      const res = Reflect.set(target, key, val, receiver);
      trigger(target, key); // re-run subscribers!
      return res;
    }
  });
}

Why Vue 3 Ditched Object.defineProperty

1 · Dynamic Keys: defineProperty had to walk all existing keys on boot. Adding a new key required Vue.set(). Proxies intercept dynamically added keys instantly.

2 · Array Mutations: Proxies intercept arr.push() and index access without monkey-patching prototype methods.

3 · Lazy Evaluation: Nested objects are only proxied when accessed, not all at initialization.

MODULE 03 · VIDEO 4
23 / 52
Lesson 4 · the cost of interception

The performance cost of interception

The V8 Optimization Barrier

V8 optimizes object access using Inline Caches (IC) and hidden classes (shapes). When a property access is trapped by a Proxy, V8 cannot generate fast-path machine code.

Accessing properties through a Proxy can be 5x to 15x slower than direct object access. Never put a Proxy inside an animation frame or a math loop.

Identity & Equality Pitfalls

proxy !== target. If a map uses objects as keys, setting the target and getting by the proxy returns undefined.

Private class fields (#private) throw a TypeError when accessed through a proxy unless bound explicitly.

Use Proxies at architectural boundaries (API client, state store, schema validation), never inside hot arithmetic or rendering loops.

Lesson 5 of 10

Encapsulation before the platform had it

For 20 years, closures were JavaScript's only tool for true private state.
// The Revealing Module Pattern (IIFE)
const CartModule = (function() {
  let items = []; // private state in closure

  function add(item) { items.push(item); }
  function count() { return items.length; }

  return { add, count }; // public API
})();

CartModule.add('Laptop');
CartModule.items; // undefined! completely private

The Mechanics of IIFE

1 · Global Namespace Isolation: Variables stay off window.

2 · Closure Memory Retention: The returned object maintains a reference to the enclosing lexical environment.

3 · Selective Exposure: Implementation details remain strictly internal.

Lesson 5 · at runtime

What 'import' actually does at runtime

// counter.js
export let count = 0;
export function inc() { count++; }

// app.js
import { count, inc } from './counter.js';

console.log(count); // 0
inc();
console.log(count); // 1 — live binding reflects update!
// count = 5; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

Three Phases of ESM Loading

  • ConstructionParse code into a Static Module Record and resolve dependencies
  • InstantiationAllocate memory locations for all exports & link bindings (no code runs yet!)
  • EvaluationExecute module code and fill the allocated memory slots with real values
CommonJS copies values; ESM links live bindings during instantiation — which is why circular imports resolve safely there and return half-built objects in CommonJS.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 5
26 / 52
Lesson 5 · what the bundler does with it

Tree-shaking & static vs dynamic import

Static Import: import { x } from './m'

Must be at the top level. Evaluated before code execution. Because the AST knows every import statically, bundlers (Rollup, Vite, Webpack) can safely eliminate unused exports (tree-shaking).

Dynamic Import: import('./m')

Returns a Promise. Evaluated on demand at runtime. Allows route-based code splitting, but cannot be analyzed for dead code before runtime.

Rule of thumb: Use static imports for core domain logic and shared types. Use dynamic import() for route chunks, heavy chart libraries, or conditional user flows.

Lesson 5 · a module instance is a singleton

Only one instance, accessible everywhere

// Implementation via ES Class + Object.freeze
let instance = null;

class DBConnection {
  constructor(uri) {
    if (instance) {
      throw new Error('Use DBConnection.getInstance()');
    }
    this.uri = uri;
    instance = this;
    Object.freeze(this);
  }

  static getInstance(uri) {
    if (!instance) instance = new DBConnection(uri);
    return instance;
  }
}

In Node/Browser Modules:

An exported object literal from an ES Module is already a singleton by default:

// logger.js
export const logger = {
  logs: [],
  log(msg) { this.logs.push(msg); }
};
Object.freeze(logger);
Because Node and browsers cache imported module instances, importing logger in 10 files gives all 10 files the exact same object reference.

28 / 52
Lesson 5 · why that bites on the server

Why senior engineers call it an anti-pattern

1 · Test Cross-Pollution

Global state lingers across test files. Test B fails because Test A mutated the singleton. Resetting state requires manual tear-down in afterEach.

2 · Hidden Dependencies

Components import the singleton directly instead of receiving it via props or DI. You cannot swap a mock client or a different config without monkey-patching.

3 · The SSR Request Leak

In Next.js / Node server runtimes, module singletons are shared across all concurrent HTTP requests. User A's session or cart leaks to User B!

In SSR and React, Singletons are a memory and security liability. Use React Provider or request-scoped Dependency Injection instead.

One object, three states, one transition

A promise settles once, and never moves again

Two consequences people miss: a promise starts executing the moment it is created, not when you await it — and attaching .then to an already-settled promise still defers to a microtask, never runs synchronously.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 6
31 / 52
The same fetch, written three ways

await is a .then you can read top to bottom

// 1 · callbacks — one nesting level per step,
//     and an error check inside each one

// 2 · promises — flat, composable
getUser(id)
  .then(getJobs)
  .then(render)
  .catch(fail)
// 3 · async/await — the same chain
async function show(id) {
  try {
    const user = await getUser(id)
    const jobs = await getJobs(user)
    render(jobs)
  } catch (e) { fail(e) }
}
These two awaits are dependent, so serial is correct. Two independent awaits written this way cost the sum of both round trips for nothing — start them together instead: await Promise.all([getJobs(), getFilters()]).
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 6
32 / 52
The four combinators, and when each is right

Pick by what failure should mean

CombinatorSettles whenUse it for
Promise.allAll fulfil — or the first rejectsData the page cannot render without. One failure should fail the screen.
Promise.allSettledEvery promise finishes, whatever the outcomeA dashboard of independent widgets. One dead endpoint must not blank the rest.
Promise.raceThe first to settle, fulfilled or rejectedTimeouts: race the request against a rejecting timer.
Promise.anyThe first to fulfil; rejects only if all doMirrors and fallbacks — take whichever source answers first.
Promise.all rejects on the first failure but does not cancel the others — they keep running and their results are discarded. Cancellation is AbortController, and it is a separate decision.

MODULE 03 · VIDEO 7
34 / 52
The try that catches nothing

A callback throws into an empty stack

try {
  setTimeout(() => {
    throw new Error('boom')
  }, 0)
} catch (e) {
  // never runs
}
By the time the callback runs, the try block has returned and its frame is gone. The throw lands on a fresh, empty stack and becomes an uncaught error on window.
// the async version — this one works
try {
  await save()      // ✓ caught
} catch (e) { report(e) }

// but this one does not
try {
  save()            // no await → unhandled rejection
} catch (e) { report(e) }
await is what re-attaches the rejection to your stack. Drop the await and you have dropped the catch with it — the single most common version of this bug.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 7
35 / 52
fetch · the rejection that never comes

A 500 is a successful request

// looks safe, ships a broken screen
const res = await fetch('/api/jobs')
const jobs = await res.json()
// 404 → res.ok false → json() throws
// "Unexpected token < in JSON"
fetch rejects only on a network failure — DNS, offline, CORS, abort. Any HTTP status your server sends, 200 to 599, is a fulfilled promise.
async function getJSON(url, opts) {
  const res = await fetch(url, opts)
  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new HttpError(res.status, url)
  }
  return res.json()
}
One wrapper, used everywhere. Now a 404 and a dropped connection arrive at the same catch, carrying enough information to tell them apart.
The same asymmetry bites in the other direction: res.json() on an empty 204 body throws, and an aborted request rejects with an AbortError you almost always want to swallow, not report.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 7
36 / 52
Where to catch, and what to say

Three boundaries, three jobs

At the call

Only if you can do something: retry, fall back to cache, use a default. Catching to console.log and continuing is how a broken screen becomes a silent one.

At the feature

One boundary per screen — an error boundary in React, one catch per route loader. It owns the user-facing message and the retry button.

At the top

unhandledrejection and window.onerror feed your telemetry. This is a smoke alarm, not a fire extinguisher — anything reaching here is a bug in the two above.

"Async errors only reach a try if the throw happens in the same turn of the loop — which for promises means I have to await them. So I put one boundary per feature, wrap fetch so an HTTP status becomes a real rejection, and let anything past that reach telemetry rather than the user."

Lesson 8 of 10 · the only rule the collector has

Garbage collection is reachability, not scope

"Out of scope" collects nothing. Unreferenced does. A leak in JavaScript is always the same thing: a reference you forgot you were still holding.

The four that cause almost all of them

  • Listeners never removedthe handler holds the closure, the closure holds the component
  • Timers never clearedsetInterval is a root until you clear it
  • Detached DOM nodesremoved from the document, still held by an array or a closure
  • Unbounded cachesa Map that only ever grows — use WeakMap when the key owns the lifetime

Lesson 8 · the leak your SPA has right now

The #1 memory leak in single-page applications

Forgetting to unsubscribe holds entire component trees hostage from Garbage Collection.

The Retained Closure Graph

When component <UserProfile /> calls eventBus.on('theme', onThemeChange), the event bus keeps a pointer to onThemeChange.

onThemeChange's closure scope references the component's state, props, and DOM nodes. When the user navigates away, the entire tree cannot be collected!

The Three Defenses

  • Always teardown in cleanupuseEffect(() => eventBus.on(..., fn), [])
  • AbortController SignalPass { signal } to native addEventListener
  • WeakRef & FinalizationRegistryFor advanced frameworks: allow GC to reclaim dead listeners

Lesson 8 · the two weak collections

When the key should own the lifetime

// strong: this Map is a root, forever
const meta = new Map()
meta.set(node, { seen: true })
node.remove()
// node is detached — and still alive,
// because meta holds it as a key

// weak: the entry dies with the node
const meta = new WeakMap()
meta.set(node, { seen: true })
node.remove()
// nothing else references node → both collected
Holds its keyIterable / sized
Map / SetYes — stronglyYes
WeakMap / WeakSetNoNo — and that is the price
Reach for WeakMap when you are annotating something you do not own: per-node metadata, per-instance private state, a memo keyed by an object argument. Reach for Map when the cache itself is the owner — and then give it a bound.
WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry exist too. Both run at the collector's convenience, not yours — worth naming in an interview, worth avoiding in application code.

Say this in the interview

Three sentences, and the recipe behind them

1 · JavaScript collects by reachability, so a leak is never "out of scope" — it is a reference I am still holding from a root.

2 · In an SPA the four usual holders are listeners, timers, detached DOM nodes and caches that only grow — so every subscription in my code returns an unsubscribe, and cleanup calls it.

3 · I confirm it rather than guess: baseline snapshot, repeat the interaction ten times, snapshot again, filter for detached nodes and read the retainer chain to the exact closure holding them.

The deliverable for this lesson is a screenshot of a retainer chain from your own app — yours, not mine. Everybody who looks, finds one.

Lesson 9 of 10 · the toolbelt, part 1

debounce
& throttle

The two most-asked utilities in frontend interviews. Both are one closure and one timer — and confusing them is the thing that gets marked.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 9
42 / 52
Say the difference before you write a line

Wait for quiet, or allow one per window

debounce(fn, wait)

Every call resets the timer. fn runs once, wait ms after the last call. Bursty input collapses to a single run.

Use for: search-as-you-type, autosave, resize-settled, validating a field after typing stops.

throttle(fn, limit)

The first call runs immediately, then further calls are ignored until the window expires. A steady stream becomes a steady rate.

Use for: scroll position, mousemove, drag, analytics pings, infinite-scroll checks.

MODULE 03 · VIDEO 9
43 / 52
Live coding · from an empty file

Both, in nine lines each

function debounce(fn, wait = 300) {
  let t                        // the closure slot
  function debounced(...args) {
    clearTimeout(t)
    t = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), wait)
  }
  debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(t)
  return debounced
}
Three details that get marked: ...args forwarded, fn.apply(this, …) so a method keeps its receiver, and a cancel for teardown.
function throttle(fn, limit = 300) {
  let last = 0, timer
  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now()
    const left = limit - (now - last)
    if (left <= 0) {
      last = now; fn.apply(this, args)      // leading
    } else if (!timer) {                   // trailing
      timer = setTimeout(() => {
        last = Date.now(); timer = null
        fn.apply(this, args)
      }, left)
    }
  }
}
Never write these as arrow functions at the top level — an arrow has no this of its own, so debounce(obj.method) silently loses its receiver. That is lesson 3, cashed in.

The follow-up questions · have the answers ready

Four things they ask after it works

QuestionThe answer
"What happens on unmount?"A pending timer still fires and touches a dead component. Return cancel and call it in cleanup — this is why the utility exposes one.
"Leading or trailing edge?"Debounce is trailing by default; throttle is leading. Say which you chose and why the other would feel wrong to the user.
"Why not requestAnimationFrame?"For anything painting per frame — scroll position, drag — rAF is the better throttle: it is aligned to the frame instead of a wall-clock guess.
"Does this fix the race?"No. Debounce reduces the number of requests; out-of-order responses still need an abort or a request id. That is module 7's autocomplete.

Lesson 10 · the distinction they probe

Observer vs Publish-Subscribe: The crucial difference

Observer Pattern

Direct Coupling: The Subject directly maintains a collection of Observer references. When something happens, the Subject iterates through them and calls their update method.

Usually synchronous and lives in the same memory context.

Publish / Subscribe (Pub-Sub)

Zero Coupling: Publishers and Subscribers never know each other exists. They communicate through a third-party Event Broker or Event Bus.

Can easily bridge asynchronous boundaries, WebSockets, or separate micro-frontends.

Interviewers love to ask: "Is Pub-Sub just the Observer pattern?" — The correct answer is: "Pub-Sub adds an independent broker channel so publishers and subscribers have zero knowledge of each other."

Lesson 10 · live coding, utility 1 of 3

Building EventEmitter from scratch

class EventEmitter {
  #events = new Map();

  on(event, listener) {
    if (!this.#events.has(event))
      this.#events.set(event, new Set());
    this.#events.get(event).add(listener);
    // senior touch: hand back the cleanup
    return () => this.off(event, listener);
  }

  emit(event, ...args) {
    const listeners = this.#events.get(event);
    if (listeners) listeners.forEach(fn => fn(...args));
  }
  off(event, listener) {
    const listeners = this.#events.get(event);
    if (listeners) listeners.delete(listener);
  }

  once(event, listener) {
    const unsub = this.on(event, (...args) => {
      unsub();
      listener(...args);
    });
    return unsub;
  }
}

// Map + Set: no duplicate listeners, O(1) off()
// #events: private — no one can mutate the registry

Lesson 10 · live coding, utility 2 of 3

deepClone — and the four things that break it

function deepClone(value, seen = new WeakMap()) {
  if (value === null || typeof value !== 'object')
    return value                    // primitives, functions
  if (seen.has(value)) return seen.get(value)

  if (value instanceof Date) return new Date(value)
  if (value instanceof Map) { /* clone entries */ }

  const out = Array.isArray(value) ? [] : {}
  seen.set(value, out)                   // before recursing
  for (const k of Reflect.ownKeys(value))
    out[k] = deepClone(value[k], seen)
  return out
}
  • Circular referencesthe WeakMap, set before the recursion — otherwise infinite
  • Non-plain objectsDate, Map, Set, RegExp all become {} if you only spread
  • Symbols and non-enumerablesReflect.ownKeys catches what Object.keys drops
In production: structuredClone() is built in, handles cycles, Map, Set and typed arrays — and throws on functions and DOM nodes. You write the manual one to prove you know what it does.

Lesson 10 · live coding, utility 3 of 3

promiseAll — a counter and an index

function promiseAll(items) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const out = []
    let pending = 0, started = 0

    for (const item of items) {
      const i = started++
      pending++
      Promise.resolve(item).then(v => {   // non-promises too
        out[i] = v                          // index, not push
        if (--pending === 0) resolve(out)
      }, reject)                            // first failure wins
    }
    if (started === 0) resolve([])       // empty input
  })
}
  • out[i] = v, never pushresults must keep input order, not completion order — this is the point of the question
  • Promise.resolve(item)the real one accepts any iterable of values, not only promises
  • Reject on the first failureand note out loud that the others keep running — rejecting is not cancelling
  • The empty array resolvesthe case that fails half of all submitted answers

Say this in the interview

Four sentences that win the architecture question

1 · I treat ES Modules as the standard module pattern — relying on static imports for tree-shaking and dynamic import() for route splitting.

2 · I avoid module singletons in modern React and SSR applications because they create testing friction and leak state across concurrent server requests.

3 · I use Proxies paired with Reflect for schema validation and reactive state tracking at system boundaries, while keeping them out of high-frequency loops.

4 · When creating thousands of data records, I prefer prototype delegation and classes to avoid closure heap duplication and unlock V8 hidden-class optimizations.
